_meta.title: Brain atlas region facts
_meta.key: region id without its prefix: ctx-lh-<label> / ctx-rh-<label> -> <label> (34 Desikan labels), deep-<name> -> <name> (10 structures)
_meta.lookup: facts[key] where key = region id without its 'ctx-lh-' / 'ctx-rh-' / 'deep-' prefix, or by_fact_key[region.fact_key] to get the same key
_meta.notice: Educational copy drafted with a text model, then rewritten and checked against standard neuroanatomy, hedged where evidence is debated. No expert or clinical review is claimed. Not medical advice. Atlas: Desikan-Killiany parcellation (Desikan et al. 2006) on a template brain; the corpus callosum label is a medial-wall boundary, not a cortical region, and is omitted.

accumbens.name: Nucleus accumbens
accumbens.function: The motivation hub: it turns dopamine-driven anticipation into drive, desire and goal pursuit.
accumbens.fact: Its activity tracks reward prediction error: it responds more to unexpected rewards than to fully predicted ones.
accumbens.clinical: Altered reward circuitry here is implicated in addiction, compulsive gambling and the anhedonia of depression.
accumbens.imaging: fMRI shows ventral striatal responses to unexpected rewards such as money, food and music.

amygdala.name: Amygdala
amygdala.function: Instantly scans your surroundings for salient threats, emotional significance, and biological survival cues.
amygdala.fact: Patients with rare bilateral amygdala calcification (Urbach-Wiethe disease) can show strikingly little fear, even when handling snakes.
amygdala.clinical: Overactivity is linked to anxiety disorders and PTSD; in monkeys, bilateral lesions produce unusual tameness.
amygdala.imaging: fMRI shows heightened responses to fearful faces, even when they are masked from awareness.

bankssts.name: Banks of the superior temporal sulcus
bankssts.function: Helps read social signals: biological motion, voices and the direction of another person's gaze.
bankssts.fact: In monkeys, neurons in the superior temporal sulcus respond to where another individual is looking; human imaging suggests a similar role in following gaze.
bankssts.clinical: Differences here are often reported in autism, alongside trouble reading gaze and vocal emotion; the findings vary between studies.
bankssts.imaging: Task-based fMRI shows activation here, building over several seconds, while people watch animated walking figures or shifting gaze.

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.function: The ancient conduit of life: it runs breathing, heart rate and arousal, and relays signals between brain and body.
brainstem.fact: Lesions only millimetres across near the pons-midbrain junction, in the reticular activating system, can cause coma.
brainstem.clinical: A ventral pons stroke can cause locked-in syndrome: awareness intact, but nearly all voluntary muscles paralysed apart from vertical eye movement and blinking.
brainstem.imaging: DTI colour maps show the descending corticospinal tracts as bright blue, vertical bundles.

caudalanteriorcingulate.name: Caudal anterior cingulate
caudalanteriorcingulate.function: Often described as the brain's internal alarm: it helps monitor cognitive conflict and is active during both physical and social pain.
caudalanteriorcingulate.fact: Social rejection and physical pain activate overlapping parts of this region on fMRI, though how specific the overlap is remains debated.
caudalanteriorcingulate.clinical: Damage or dysfunction here is linked to apathy and, with bilateral lesions, akinetic mutism; it is also implicated in severe obsessive-compulsive disorder.
caudalanteriorcingulate.imaging: fMRI activity here rises during Stroop-type conflict tasks and when people notice their own errors.

caudalmiddlefrontal.name: Caudal middle frontal
caudalmiddlefrontal.function: Links planning to action: it helps prepare movements and steer the eyes during deliberate visual attention.
caudalmiddlefrontal.fact: The frontal eye fields lie at or near this region; electrical stimulation there makes the eyes jump toward the opposite side.
caudalmiddlefrontal.clinical: An acute lesion can make both eyes deviate toward the damaged side, usually improving over days to weeks.
caudalmiddlefrontal.imaging: fMRI activity here rises during visual search and the planning of eye and hand movements.

caudate.name: Caudate nucleus
caudate.function: A C-shaped nucleus curving around the thalamus that steers goal-directed action, learning and mental flexibility.
caudate.fact: Its name is Latin for tail: a plump head bulges into the lateral ventricle, then the body tapers into a long tail that arcs back toward the temporal lobe.
caudate.clinical: Loss of its medium spiny neurons is the hallmark of Huntington's disease, causing involuntary movements and cognitive decline.
caudate.imaging: On T1 MRI it is a grey-matter ridge lining the walls of the lateral ventricles, which makes it easy to outline in volume studies.

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.function: Tucked under the cortex, it fine-tunes balance, movement and timing by comparing predicted with actual sensory feedback.
cerebellum.fact: It holds only about 10 percent of the brain's volume but roughly 80 percent of its neurons.
cerebellum.clinical: Damage causes ataxia: unsteady, uncoordinated movement, intention tremor and misjudged reach (dysmetria) without true weakness.
cerebellum.imaging: DTI tractography shows the cerebellar peduncles, the thick fibre bundles linking the cerebellum with brainstem and cortex.

cuneus.name: Cuneus
cuneus.function: Receives input from the upper retina, so it represents the lower half of the visual field.
cuneus.fact: Bound between the parieto-occipital and calcarine fissures, this region takes its name from the Latin word for 'wedge.'
cuneus.clinical: A stroke here can cause a lower quadrantanopia: loss of sight in the lower opposite quarter of the visual field.
cuneus.imaging: T1 MRI shows its wedge on the medial surface; DTI traces the optic radiation ending in the calcarine cortex beside it.

entorhinal.name: Entorhinal cortex
entorhinal.function: The gateway to the hippocampus: it maps space with internal grids and funnels sensory experience into memory.
entorhinal.fact: Grid cells here fire in a repeating hexagonal pattern that acts like a built-in coordinate system; their discovery in rats earned a 2014 Nobel Prize.
entorhinal.clinical: Among the first areas to develop the tangles of Alzheimer's disease, often before memory loss is obvious.
entorhinal.imaging: In group studies, high-resolution MRI has shown thinning here years before a dementia diagnosis; it is not a reliable test for any one person.

frontalpole.name: Frontal pole
frontalpole.function: Sits at the very front of the brain and helps juggle several goals at once, holding an intention in mind while you attend to something else.
frontalpole.fact: Part of the prefrontal cortex, which matures later than most of the brain: myelination and cortical pruning continue into the twenties.
frontalpole.clinical: Frontopolar damage can leave people able to follow instructions yet poor at multitasking and at carrying out multi-step plans.
frontalpole.imaging: Comparative MRI suggests it is disproportionately large in humans compared with other apes; fMRI links it to tasks that need switching between goals.

fusiform.name: Fusiform gyrus
fusiform.function: A ventral visual hub that sorts what you see into categories, most famously turning faces into recognisable identities.
fusiform.fact: Its face-selective patch may also be recruited by visual expertise, as in bird watchers or car enthusiasts, though this is debated.
fusiform.clinical: Damage to this region, often on both sides, can cause prosopagnosia (face blindness): familiar faces look unfamiliar.
fusiform.imaging: fMRI shows a face-selective patch, the fusiform face area, responding more to faces than to houses or objects.

hippocampus.name: Hippocampus
hippocampus.function: Central to forming new long-term memories and to spatial navigation.
hippocampus.fact: In London taxi drivers the posterior hippocampus is larger, and the difference tracks how many years they have spent learning the city's streets.
hippocampus.clinical: Bilateral damage can cause profound anterograde amnesia: new episodic memories fail to form, as in the famous patient H.M.
hippocampus.imaging: High-resolution T2-weighted MRI can resolve its curled subfields, such as CA1 and the dentate gyrus.

inferiorparietal.name: Inferior parietal
inferiorparietal.function: Acts as a multimodal crossroads, weaving attention, language, and mathematical calculation into a unified conscious experience.
inferiorparietal.fact: A 1999 post-mortem study of Einstein's brain reported unusually wide inferior parietal regions, though the interpretation is debated.
inferiorparietal.clinical: Right-hemisphere lesions here can cause hemispatial neglect: patients may fail to notice things on their left side.
inferiorparietal.imaging: Diffusion imaging shows dense white-matter links between this hub and frontal language and attention regions.

inferiortemporal.name: Inferior temporal
inferiortemporal.function: A visual catalogue that assembles shapes, contours and colours into recognisable objects.
inferiortemporal.fact: Neurons here largely keep their object preference when an object changes size or position, helping you recognise a cup from many angles.
inferiortemporal.clinical: Damage can cause visual agnosia: seeing an object clearly yet being unable to recognise or name it.
inferiortemporal.imaging: fMRI shows category-selective patches along this cortex for tools, animals and everyday objects.

insula.name: Insula
insula.function: Translates internal bodily states like heartbeat, gut sensations, and temperature into subjective emotional feelings and gut instincts.
insula.fact: In a 2007 study, smokers with insula damage from stroke were far more likely to quit easily and lose the urge to smoke.
insula.clinical: Insular degeneration, as in some frontotemporal dementias, can blunt empathy and the recognition of disgust.
insula.imaging: Resting-state fMRI identifies the anterior insula as an anchor of the salience network, coordinating switches between internal and external attention.

isthmuscingulate.name: Isthmus cingulate
isthmuscingulate.function: Serves as a crucial spatial and memory bridge linking the cingulate gyrus to the parahippocampal cortex.
isthmuscingulate.fact: Though small, this strip behind the corpus callosum is thought to link spatial navigation with episodic memory.
isthmuscingulate.clinical: Thinning here has been associated with mild cognitive impairment that later converts to Alzheimer's disease.
isthmuscingulate.imaging: DTI traces the cingulum bundle fibres that run through this region toward the temporal lobe.

lateraloccipital.name: Lateral occipital
lateraloccipital.function: Assembles fragmented edges, textures, and contours into recognizable, coherent visual shapes and everyday objects.
lateraloccipital.fact: It contains the lateral occipital complex, which responds to object shape whether sensed by sight or by touch.
lateraloccipital.clinical: Focal damage can cause visual object agnosia: patients see, but fail to recognise everyday objects by sight alone.
lateraloccipital.imaging: On fMRI, it shows selective BOLD signal increases when subjects view intact objects compared to scrambled geometric noise.

lateralorbitofrontal.name: Lateral orbitofrontal
lateralorbitofrontal.function: This region evaluates changing rules and suppresses choices that no longer yield beneficial outcomes.
lateralorbitofrontal.fact: It often responds when a once-rewarding cue stops paying off or starts to be punished, as in reversal-learning tasks.
lateralorbitofrontal.clinical: Lesions can cause perseveration: patients keep repeating a strategy that no longer works.
lateralorbitofrontal.imaging: Air-filled sinuses nearby cause signal dropout in fMRI here, so tilted slices are often used to recover the signal.

lingual.name: Lingual gyrus
lingual.function: Helps process colour and shape in the ventral visual stream and supports recognising visual landmarks.
lingual.fact: Its name comes from the Latin lingua, tongue, for its tongue-like shape; it lies below the calcarine sulcus and processes the upper half of the visual field.
lingual.clinical: Lesions here and in the adjacent fusiform gyrus can cause cerebral achromatopsia: the world loses colour and looks grey.
lingual.imaging: T1 MRI shows it as a gyrus below the calcarine sulcus; fMRI responds to colour, landmark and scene tasks.

medialorbitofrontal.name: Medial orbitofrontal
medialorbitofrontal.function: It calculates the subjective, moment-to-moment value of rewards like delicious food, social approval, and aesthetic beauty.
medialorbitofrontal.fact: In taste experiments, activity here rose when people believed a wine was expensive, even when it was the same wine.
medialorbitofrontal.clinical: Damage can lead to socially inappropriate choices, poor economic decision-making, and an inability to weigh future consequences.
medialorbitofrontal.imaging: Resting-state fMRI shows strong functional connectivity with the default mode network, though sinus air pockets can cause signal loss.

middletemporal.name: Middle temporal
middletemporal.function: Contributes to word meaning and semantic memory; its posterior part helps process visual motion.
middletemporal.fact: It tends to activate when you classify tools, tell animals apart or process action verbs, as if consulting a mental encyclopedia.
middletemporal.clinical: Atrophy of the anterior temporal lobe, including this gyrus, can cause semantic dementia, in which objects lose their meaning.
middletemporal.imaging: Structural MRI measures cortical thinning here to follow decline in semantic dementia.

pallidum.name: Globus pallidus
pallidum.function: The basal ganglia's brake: it suppresses unwanted muscle contractions so intended movements can proceed smoothly.
pallidum.fact: It is one of the most iron-rich parts of the brain, which is why it looks dark on susceptibility-weighted MRI.
pallidum.clinical: Carbon monoxide poisoning can damage it, sometimes causing delayed parkinsonism and apathy.
pallidum.imaging: Its iron content gives strong signal loss on T2* and susceptibility-weighted MRI.

paracentral.name: Paracentral lobule
paracentral.lobe_or_system: Frontal lobe (medial surface; the lobule straddles the central sulcus)
paracentral.function: A medial patch where the motor and sensory strips meet; it controls and senses the legs and feet and is thought to help control bladder and bowel.
paracentral.fact: It straddles the central sulcus on the medial surface: its front part is mainly motor and its back part mainly somatosensory.
paracentral.clinical: Ischemia from anterior cerebral artery strokes can cause contralateral leg weakness paired with unexpected, sudden urinary incontinence.
paracentral.imaging: Midline sagittal T1 MRI shows it where the central sulcus reaches the medial surface, just above the cingulate sulcus.

parahippocampal.name: Parahippocampal gyrus
parahippocampal.function: Encodes scenes and spatial layout, anchoring memories to the places where they happened.
parahippocampal.fact: A subregion, the parahippocampal place area, responds more to scenes, rooms and landscapes than to faces.
parahippocampal.clinical: Damage can cause topographical disorientation (landmark agnosia): getting lost in familiar places despite normal vision.
parahippocampal.imaging: fMRI reliably lights this gyrus up when people view photographs of streets, rooms or landscapes.

parsopercularis.name: Pars opercularis (Broca's area)
parsopercularis.function: Coordinates the physical mechanics of speech, transforming abstract thoughts into complex vocal and motor articulatory patterns.
parsopercularis.fact: Part of Broca's area, it shows mirror-like responses: active both when you produce speech gestures and when you watch someone else make them.
parsopercularis.clinical: Left-hemisphere damage here and nearby can cause Broca's (expressive) aphasia: effortful, halting speech with comprehension largely preserved.
parsopercularis.imaging: DTI tractography shows the arcuate fasciculus linking this area with posterior language regions, a loop used when repeating speech.

parsorbitalis.name: Pars orbitalis
parsorbitalis.function: Helps retrieve and select word meanings, linking language to context in the lower front of the inferior frontal gyrus.
parsorbitalis.fact: Though often grouped with Broca's area, it is more often linked to meaning (semantic retrieval) than to the mechanics of speech.
parsorbitalis.clinical: Damage in the left inferior frontal gyrus can make it hard to pick the right word or meaning.
parsorbitalis.imaging: Left-hemisphere fMRI activity rises here during tasks that require choosing between competing word meanings.

parstriangularis.name: Pars triangularis (Broca's area)
parstriangularis.function: Helps select the right word and build grammatical sentences, filtering out competing meanings.
parstriangularis.fact: Pars triangularis is often larger in the left hemisphere than the right, a leftward asymmetry linked to language dominance, though it varies between people.
parstriangularis.clinical: Left-hemisphere damage here and nearby can cause halting, non-fluent speech with simplified grammar.
parstriangularis.imaging: fMRI activity rises in this area during sentence reading and when a task forces a choice between competing word meanings.

pericalcarine.name: Pericalcarine (primary visual cortex)
pericalcarine.function: Acts as vision's primary gateway, deconstructing incoming light into raw orientation, spatial frequency, and contrast coordinates.
pericalcarine.fact: A thick myelinated stripe called the line of Gennari runs through layer IV, visible to the naked eye upon dissection.
pericalcarine.clinical: Damage on both sides causes cortical blindness, though some patients show blindsight, reacting to stimuli they report not seeing.
pericalcarine.imaging: Retinotopic fMRI maps the visual field across this cortex in an orderly, inverted layout; ultra-high-field scanners can resolve column-scale detail.

postcentral.name: Postcentral gyrus (somatosensory)
postcentral.function: This strip transforms raw touches, temperatures, and pain signals from across your body into conscious sensory awareness.
postcentral.fact: Sensory inputs are mapped upside-down, dedicating disproportionately massive cortical real estate to your sensitive lips and fingertips.
postcentral.clinical: Damage often impairs tactile discrimination and proprioception on the opposite side of the body without fully abolishing coarse touch sensation.
postcentral.imaging: Structural MRI clearly defines it behind the central sulcus, while fMRI registers peak BOLD signals seconds after tactile skin stimulation.

posteriorcingulate.name: Posterior cingulate
posteriorcingulate.function: A hub of the default mode network, linked to autobiographical memory and to whether attention points inward or outward.
posteriorcingulate.fact: Its activity dips when you focus on a demanding task and rises again when your mind wanders.
posteriorcingulate.clinical: Reduced metabolism here is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease on PET imaging.
posteriorcingulate.imaging: Structural MRI shows cortical thinning in early dementia, while resting-state fMRI maps its DMN connectivity.

precentral.name: Precentral gyrus (motor)
precentral.function: It generates and dispatches the final neural commands that drive voluntary, skilled muscle contractions across the body.
precentral.fact: It holds the famous motor homunculus, a body map in which the hands and face get disproportionately large territory.
precentral.clinical: Strokes affecting this gyrus cause contralateral hemiparesis or focal paralysis, stripping away voluntary fine-motor control.
precentral.imaging: Diffusion tensor imaging traces its massive corticospinal tract through the internal capsule down into the brainstem.

precuneus.name: Precuneus
precuneus.function: Linked to self-reflection, taking a first-person perspective and vivid mental imagery; a hub of the default mode network.
precuneus.fact: With the posterior cingulate it is among the most metabolically active cortical regions at rest, humming along when the mind wanders.
precuneus.clinical: Reduced metabolism and amyloid build-up here are among the earliest imaging changes in Alzheimer's disease.
precuneus.imaging: Resting-state fMRI identifies it as an exceptionally connected core hub within the default mode network.

putamen.name: Putamen
putamen.function: A dense hub that automates learned movements, turning conscious effort into fluent habit.
putamen.fact: Its name is Latin for 'husk' or 'shell'; with the globus pallidus it forms the lentiform nucleus.
putamen.clinical: Dopamine loss here underlies the slowness and rigidity of Parkinson's disease; the circuit is also implicated in Tourette syndrome.
putamen.imaging: Iron builds up in the putamen with age, so it looks darker on T2-weighted and susceptibility-weighted MRI.

rostralanteriorcingulate.name: Rostral anterior cingulate
rostralanteriorcingulate.function: Thought to help regulate emotion by damping amygdala responses and weighing distressing impulses against goals.
rostralanteriorcingulate.fact: Activity here before treatment has been found to predict which people with major depression respond to antidepressants, a marker still under study.
rostralanteriorcingulate.clinical: Altered activity here is implicated in depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
rostralanteriorcingulate.imaging: PET and fMRI studies show altered activity here in depression; DTI suggests changed links with prefrontal cortex.

rostralmiddlefrontal.name: Rostral middle frontal
rostralmiddlefrontal.function: A hub for working memory, planning and weighing options; it overlaps the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
rostralmiddlefrontal.fact: Prefrontal cortex is proportionally larger in humans than in other primates, which is thought to support abstract, hypothetical reasoning.
rostralmiddlefrontal.clinical: The overlapping dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is the usual target of magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for treatment-resistant depression.
rostralmiddlefrontal.imaging: Diffusion MRI traces dense white-matter links between here and parietal cortex in the frontoparietal control network.

superiorfrontal.name: Superior frontal
superiorfrontal.function: Supports working memory, movement planning and cognitive control; its medial strip helps start voluntary actions.
superiorfrontal.fact: Its medial strip holds the supplementary motor area, active both when you move and when you merely imagine moving.
superiorfrontal.clinical: Lesions of the medial frontal region can cause alien hand syndrome, in which a limb acts as if it has a will of its own.
superiorfrontal.imaging: fMRI shows supplementary-motor activity for planned and imagined movements; the medial part also belongs to the default-mode network.

superiorparietal.name: Superior parietal
superiorparietal.function: Integrates sensory and visual signals to construct an ongoing internal map of where your body exists in space.
superiorparietal.fact: Parietal cortex including this area supports stereognosis, recognising a coin or key in your pocket by touch alone.
superiorparietal.clinical: Damage can cause optic ataxia, leaving a person able to see an object clearly yet unable to reach out and grasp it.
superiorparietal.imaging: Functional MRI shows activation in this region during mental rotation of 3D objects.

superiortemporal.name: Superior temporal (auditory, Wernicke)
superiortemporal.function: Turns sound into music and speech; its posterior part (Wernicke's area) is key to understanding spoken language.
superiortemporal.fact: Auditory cortex on its upper surface keeps a tonotopic map: sound frequencies laid out in order, a little like piano keys.
superiortemporal.clinical: Damage to its posterior part, usually on the left, can cause Wernicke's aphasia: fluent, effortless speech that makes little sense, with poor comprehension.
superiortemporal.imaging: High-resolution fMRI resolves frequency gradients in Heschl's gyrus; DTI traces the arcuate fasciculus running forward to frontal language areas.

supramarginal.name: Supramarginal gyrus
supramarginal.function: Supports phonological processing in language and, on the right, is thought to help separate your own feelings from other people's.
supramarginal.fact: Right supramarginal activity has been linked to overcoming egocentric bias: judging others' feelings without projecting your own.
supramarginal.clinical: Left-hemisphere lesions here can cause conduction aphasia or phonological reading problems, with difficulty repeating what was heard.
supramarginal.imaging: fMRI highlights this region when individuals must rapidly distinguish real words from nonsense pseudo-words.

temporalpole.name: Temporal pole
temporalpole.function: Perched at the temporal tip, it joins sights, sounds and emotions into concepts, autobiographical memory and social understanding.
temporalpole.fact: It acts as a semantic hub, likely binding abstract facts to emotional tone to help decipher other people's hidden social intentions.
temporalpole.clinical: Degeneration of the anterior temporal lobe, including the pole, causes semantic dementia: word and object meanings fade.
temporalpole.imaging: Diffusion MRI shows the uncinate fasciculus linking the temporal pole with orbitofrontal cortex, a route implicated in social and emotional processing.

thalamus.name: Thalamus
thalamus.function: A central relay that routes sensory signals to the cortex and takes part in attention and arousal.
thalamus.fact: Almost all sensory data passes through its gates, except smell, which largely bypasses it initially.
thalamus.clinical: Thalamic stroke can cause sensory loss or severe central pain; thalamic degeneration is central to fatal familial insomnia.
thalamus.imaging: DTI tractography shows thalamocortical fibres radiating outward to the cortex.

transversetemporal.name: Transverse temporal (Heschl's gyrus)
transversetemporal.function: Buried in the lateral fissure, this is primary auditory cortex: it receives sound from the ears and begins decoding pitch and timbre.
transversetemporal.fact: Heschl's gyrus holds a map of sound frequency, with low to high pitches laid out in ordered gradients, like a keyboard.
transversetemporal.clinical: Damage on both sides can cause cortical deafness: the ears work, but sound is not consciously perceived.
transversetemporal.imaging: Tractography can follow auditory fibres from the thalamus toward Heschl's gyrus, though this is technically difficult.

ventricles.name: Ventricular system
ventricles.function: The fluid-filled cavities deep in the brain (lateral, third and fourth ventricles) cushion it and circulate cerebrospinal fluid, made largely by the choroid plexus.
ventricles.fact: Cerebrospinal fluid is renewed several times a day; the textbook route drains it through arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses, though other routes are debated.
ventricles.clinical: Blockages in fluid pathways cause hydrocephalus, producing elevated intracranial pressure that can expand these chambers and damage adjacent brain tissue.
ventricles.imaging: T2-weighted MRI displays these chambers as brilliantly bright pockets of fluid that sharply contrast with surrounding darker neural tissue.
